summary: A Mobile IPv6 node needs a home address, a home agent address and a security association with the home agent before it can register. This informational document discusses the problems of obtaining that information, called bootstrapping, and several deployment scenarios in which it must happen.

eli5.summary: Before you can get mail forwarded while traveling, you need your permanent address, the post office's address and a secret password. This explains how to get those three things in the first place.

subtitle: Why a Mobile IPv6 device needs help learning its home address, home agent and keys, and what has to be true for that to work.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 assumes a mobile node already holds a home address, a home agent address and a security association with the home agent. Provisioning all of this by hand does not work well in real deployments.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines bootstrapping as obtaining that information, sets design goals and non-goals, describes the roles of access and mobility providers, and walks through deployment scenarios and the minimal seed parameters each one provides.
tldr.outcome: It is only a problem statement. It stops short of suggesting preferred solutions and leaves those to separate documents.

facts.label: Must be obtained
facts.value: Home agent address, home address, IPsec SA with the HA

today: RFC 4640 is an Informational problem statement and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It deliberately stops short of recommending solutions, which the text says would come from separate documents.

sections.title: What Bootstrapping Means
sections.content:
RFC 3775 defines Mobile IPv6 and assumes a mobile node (MN) has a trust relationship with an entity called the home agent (HA). Signaling between the two is secured with IPsec or with the authentication protocol of RFC 4285. The base specification implicitly requires the MN to be provisioned with enough information to register with its home agent, and static provisioning causes practical deployment issues.

Bootstrapping is the process of obtaining enough information at the mobile node that it can register with an appropriate home agent. Concretely, that means getting the home agent address and the home address, and having the MN and HA authenticate each other and build security credentials for Mobile IPv6.

It typically happens when the node has no information at first boot or keeps none across reboots. After the first time, how often to repeat it is implementation dependent: on every boot, on every prefix change, or periodically to anchor to a better home agent.
sections.eli5: Bootstrapping is the first-day setup. Your device has to find out its permanent address, who its helper is, and how to prove it is really you.

sections.title: Design Goals and Non-Goals
sections.content:
A solution must leave the MN with three things: the home agent address, the home address, and an IPsec security association between MN and HA, including an IKE pre-shared secret. Bootstrapping can be triggered at any time by the MN or the network, even when the MN is already registered, for example to refresh credentials.

  • Later interactions, such as updating the security association, can happen between MN and HA without involving the bootstrapping infrastructure.
  • Solutions should allow user-specific information to be stored on entities other than the home agent.
  • Configuration exchanged between MN and HA must have integrity and replay protection, and confidentiality if necessary.
  • The solution should fit all feasible deployment scenarios and their authentication and authorization models.

Two things are explicitly out of scope. Home prefix renumbering is not specially supported, although re-running bootstrapping at every power-on takes care of it. Bootstrapping with no trust relationship between the MN and any provider is not considered.
sections.eli5: A good fix has to hand over the address, the helper and the secret, let you redo it any time, and keep the secret safe on the way.

sections.title: Why Static Setup Falls Short
sections.content:
The default bootstrapping in the base specification binds tightly to specific home and home agent addresses. The RFC lists several problems.

Home address. The home agent uses the home address for authorization, and Mobile IPv6 uses IKEv1, which cannot update the security policy database for a dynamically assigned home address. So static assignment is the only technique compatible with the base specification. Dynamic assignment would help with DHCP-based assignment, recovery from duplicate address collisions, addressing privacy, ease of deployment and prefix changes in the home network.

Home agent. The home agent address sits in the security policy database, and multiple home agents need multiple entries. Dynamic assignment would support independent network management, local home agents and load balancing. The home agent discovery protocol also has no local discovery mechanism in an access provider's network.

Security and topology. IKEv1-based key exchange has no integration with backend AAA infrastructure unless certificates or pre-shared secrets are used, and the RFC notes that IKEv2 does provide this. Dormant mobile nodes, which may be asleep or switched off, miss prefix updates pushed to them.
sections.eli5: Writing every address and password by hand is like hand-labeling every suitcase. It breaks the moment something moves, and nobody can fix it for the traveler.

sections.title: Access and Mobility Service Roles
sections.content:
The RFC separates two services. Network access service lets a host send and receive IP packets and is provided by an access service provider (ASP). Mobility service is Mobile IPv6 itself and is provided by a mobility service provider (MSP). Each service has an authorizer: the access service authorizer (ASA) and the mobility service authorizer (MSA).

When one operator both authorizes and provides mobility service it is the home MSP; if another provides it, that operator is the serving MSP, which must check with the MSA before granting service. The same split applies to network access, which is how roaming works. The RFC gives the example of a business traveler at an airport hotspot whose provider has a roaming agreement with the traveler's cellular provider.

Many combinations are possible, such as the serving ASP also being the home MSP, and all reasonable ones must be considered because they affect home agent discovery, home address configuration and MN-to-HA authentication.
sections.eli5: The company that lets you use the road is not always the company that gives you the forwarding service. The roles can be split in many ways, and the setup has to work for all of them.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios and Seed Parameters
sections.content:
All scenarios assume a trust relationship between the mobile user and the MSA, usually with the AAA in the MSA's network. The RFC describes four.

  • Mobility service subscription: the MN subscribes to a home MSP and is configured out of band with an identity and credentials, such as an NAI and shared secret. It should be able to bootstrap from any access location.
  • Integrated ASP network: the ASA and MSA are the same entity, so the credentials for network access can also bootstrap MIPv6.
  • Third-party MSP: the subscription is with one entity (for example a corporate network) but the service comes from another, a serving MSP, with transitive trust between them.
  • Infrastructure-less: no relationship exists between host and infrastructure, for example the IETF meeting network. This scenario is not supported, for reasons given in the security section.

The seed parameters depend on whether network access authentication is independent of mobility authentication. In Parameter Set 1 the MN may need the home agent's domain name (or FQDN) to discover its address, and IKE credentials to authenticate with it. In Parameter Set 2 a security association from network access authentication is reused, and all required information is bootstrapped from the network access credentials.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you sign up with one company, sometimes the same company runs everything, sometimes two companies team up, and sometimes nobody knows you at all. Each case starts from a different small clue.

sections.title: Security of Bootstrapping
sections.content:
There are two aspects: the security required of the outcome by RFC 3775, and the security of the process itself. The outcome must establish IPsec security associations in a way where authenticity is proved and confidentiality ensured, ideally with key material known only to the home agent and mobile node. RFC 3775 also requires a trust relationship, so infrastructure-less solutions are out of scope, and a home address must be authorized to one host at a time.

The listed threats include a bogus home agent address or bogus security associations offered by an attacker, a fake mobile node trying to steal service, a man in the middle stealing credentials, and a distributed denial-of-service attack on the bootstrapping entity.

Keys for network access and for mobility service must be cryptographically separate, separately named and have separate lifetimes, even when generated from the same credentials. Cryptographic processes must also allow multiple algorithms.
sections.eli5: Setup is the easiest moment for a thief to trick you with a fake helper or a stolen password. So the secret must be shared only with the right helper, and the network and forwarding passwords must stay separate.
